title: German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty
subtitle: Turning conquest into a settlement
body:
On 28 September 1939, Warsaw formally surrendered to the German army. In Moscow, the governments responsible for Poland’s invasion were completing an agreement about what would follow its defeat. Joachim von Ribbentrop and Vyacheslav Molotov gave their settlement a reassuring name: the German–Soviet Boundary and Friendship Treaty. The friendship belonged to the signatories. The boundary would run through someone else’s country.

The coincidence mattered, but it could mislead. Warsaw’s capitulation was a military surrender, not a Polish signature on the partition of the republic. The treaty proceeded from the claim that Poland had ceased to exist and that Germany and the Soviet Union could therefore arrange its affairs between themselves. Polish representatives rejected that claim. Within days, they were explaining abroad that losing control of the national territory had not transferred the right to dispose of it to the invading powers. The dispute concerned the survival of a state as well as the fate of its land. [1] [2] The preceding studies have followed the [August pact](/articles/molotov-ribbentrop-pact-1939-08-23), the [German attack](/articles/german-invasion-poland-1939-09-01) and the [Soviet invasion](/articles/soviet-invasion-poland-1939-09-17). Their consequences now converged around a negotiating table. Armies had created the opportunity for partition; diplomacy was being used to make the results appear orderly, durable and defensible. Yet the agreement extended well beyond a line on a map. Its accompanying documents concerned Lithuania, Polish political activity, population movements, raw materials and the attempt to persuade Britain and France to stop fighting. Warsaw’s capitulation did not end the campaign. Modlin held until **29 September**, the Hel Peninsula until **2 October**, and organized fighting continued around Kock until **6 October**. These later dates matter to the meaning of the agreement: the governments in Moscow were claiming political finality while Polish troops still resisted. A capitulation could bind the forces surrendering at a particular place without authorizing two foreign states to extinguish Poland. The treaty’s assertion of settlement consequently ran ahead of events on the battlefield as well as against the position maintained by Polish diplomacy. [3] [4]

Returning to Moscow with a different bargain

The secret protocol of 23 August had left some matters open. It envisaged a division of interests in Polish territory approximately along the Narew, Vistula and San, but reserved the question of whether an independent Polish state should survive. That reservation was disappearing by late September. In a telegram describing his meeting with Stalin and Molotov on 25 September, the German ambassador, Friedrich-Werner von der Schulenburg, reported Stalin’s opposition to leaving a Polish rump state. Stalin presented such a state as a potential cause of future disagreement between the two powers. This was a German diplomatic account of the conversation, but it recorded a specific proposal subsequently reflected in the settlement. [5] [6] Stalin offered Germany the Lublin province and the part of Warsaw province extending to the Bug, in exchange for relinquishing German claims to Lithuania. His intervention helps explain why the eventual boundary differed from the August arrangement. The revision was not simply the result of German troops having advanced farther than anticipated. Soviet leadership was actively bargaining over the shape of the occupation and the direction in which Soviet influence should expand. Berlin gained a larger share of central Poland; Moscow gained German acceptance of its predominant interest in Lithuania. The same conversation linked agreement over Poland to further Soviet action in the Baltic region. [6] Ribbentrop arrived in Moscow on the evening of 27 September. A timetable preserved among the papers of German diplomat Andor Hencke places the first meeting that night and further discussions on the following afternoon. Dinner at the Kremlin and an act of *Swan Lake* interrupted the schedule before talks resumed at midnight. The brief record places the signing at five in the morning, after that resumption. The documents nevertheless bear the date 28 September, which is the treaty’s historical and legal date. This small discrepancy between the calendar of the talks and the date written on the agreement is a reminder that diplomatic anniversaries often compress negotiations that continued through the night. [7]

What five public articles tried to settle

The public treaty was short enough to conceal its ambition behind administrative language. Article I identified the boundary of German and Soviet interests through an attached map, with further description to follow. Article II declared the line definitive and rejected intervention by other powers. Article III assigned administrative reorganization west of the line to Germany and east of it to the Soviet Union. Article IV presented the settlement as a basis for friendship between their peoples. Article V required ratification but made the agreement effective upon signature. The preamble’s reference to the “former Polish state” was the political premise supporting the whole construction. [8] A reader could easily mistake this language for the record of a negotiated peace. No Polish government had agreed to the terms. No provision asked the population whether it accepted either administration. The treaty instead treated the invaders’ capacity to occupy territory as sufficient authority to reorganize it. Its claim to finality was also directed outward: other governments were being told that the Polish question had been removed from legitimate international discussion. That was a political demand whose acceptance still had to be won, rather than a fact established by the signatures. [8] [2] The revised division placed much of the central stretch of the boundary on the Bug, farther east than the earlier Vistula division. A report sent from Berlin by the American chargé, Alexander Kirk, on 29 September described the published route from the vicinity of Lithuania through the northern river system, along the Bug and eventually to the San. It was a report of the German news agency’s description, rather than a field survey. Its value lies in showing what was being announced to the outside world: the partners had replaced a provisional arrangement with a declared territorial settlement, including a new allocation of land in central Poland. [9] Even then, a line declared definitive still needed practical definition. On 5 October, Steinhardt reported that Molotov and Schulenburg had signed the supplementary protocol the previous day and that a mixed commission would work on the frontier’s details. His later dispatch recorded ratification by the Soviet and German authorities on 19 October. Signature, ratification and demarcation were therefore separate events. The treaty could take effect between its signatories before surveyors and officials completed the work of implementing it. For residents, those successive steps could determine when an anticipated division became a guarded crossing or a change of administration. [10] [11]

Reading the atlas

A partition line is not a battlefront

The 28 September map shows an approximate trace of the agreed partition. It should not be read as proof that all troops had reached their final positions that day. The later demarcation work also means that the treaty date and the physical marking of the frontier must be kept separate. A diplomatic map records what governments agreed to claim; an operational map must establish where forces actually were. [10]

Lithuania in the balance

The territorial revision had another side that remained secret. Lithuania was transferred into the Soviet sphere of influence, while Germany acquired the specified additional Polish territory. The supplementary protocol also preserved a prospective German claim to a strip in southwestern Lithuania and protected existing German–Lithuanian economic agreements. These details expose the transactional character of the bargain. Lithuania was neither a defeated participant in the Polish campaign nor a consenting party to this agreement. Its future was being discussed as something two larger neighbors could exchange for advantages elsewhere. [12] This was an allocation of influence, not the immediate annexation of Lithuania. That distinction mattered because coercion would proceed through further steps, with their own documents and public explanations. On 10 October, Lithuania concluded a mutual assistance treaty with the Soviet Union. In return for Vilnius and its surrounding district, the agreement permitted Soviet bases and garrisons on Lithuanian territory. Steinhardt’s report the following morning noted that their numbers and locations were to be settled separately. Moscow was able to attach a powerful inducement to a grave restriction of Lithuanian freedom of action: the recovery of a city Lithuania claimed, but which had been under Polish rule before the invasion. [13] For Poles from Wilno, as the city was known in Polish, this meant another decision about their home made without Polish participation. For Lithuania, the agreement joined a national aspiration to the presence of a larger power’s troops. The Soviet occupation and incorporation of Lithuania in 1940 followed later; it should not be moved backward into September 1939. The sequence is nevertheless revealing. A secret understanding between Berlin and Moscow narrowed the space in which a smaller state could negotiate, and subsequent agreements converted that imbalance into military access and eventually the loss of independence. [14] The southwestern strip remained a source of private maneuvering. Ribbentrop’s instructions of 4 October, transmitted early on 5 October, recorded that Molotov had informed the Lithuanian foreign minister of the confidential arrangement. Berlin now had to explain its own claim. The instructions presented the proposed transfer as a practical correction to an awkward border, while reserving Germany’s right to decide when it should occur. Germany also wanted Soviet troops kept out of the strip. The episode shows how a settlement advertised as clear and final could still contain deferred claims, controlled disclosures and competing preferences over implementation. [15]

A smaller state’s predicament

The price attached to Vilnius

The October agreement offered Lithuania a long-sought city together with Soviet military installations. Those terms should be read together. The territorial gain helped make a coercive strategic arrangement presentable as a diplomatic success. Neither the transfer of Vilnius nor the secret allocation of Lithuania’s sphere represented Polish consent to the disposal of territory. [13]

Polish politics and populations behind the new line

Another secret protocol addressed the possibility that Poles might refuse to accept the settlement in practice. Each government undertook to suppress Polish agitation in its territory when that activity affected the other party’s territory, and to inform its partner about suitable measures. The clause was brief, but its political meaning was substantial. The occupiers understood that an imposed boundary would not necessarily divide Polish loyalties or the desire to restore independence. They promised cooperation against a form of activity that could connect opposition on both sides. [16] The wording should be taken seriously without being made to prove more than it says. It establishes an undertaking to suppress the specified political activity and exchange information about measures against it. It does not itself document particular police conferences, joint operations or the origins of every subsequent crime. Those questions require their own records. The direct evidence is already consequential: a public promise of order was accompanied by a secret commitment to restrict Polish efforts that threatened the partner’s control. The settlement’s security depended in part on preventing the people it excluded from reopening the question of their own state. [16] A confidential population protocol approached the inhabitants from a different direction. Moscow agreed not to obstruct the departure of German nationals and people of German descent who wished to move to Germany or German-administered territory. Transfers were to be conducted by German agents working with the local authorities, with emigrants’ property rights protected. Berlin assumed a corresponding obligation for people of Ukrainian or Belarusian descent in its area. The document’s language concerned people wishing to migrate. It was not a blanket authorization for every forced displacement that followed. Yet its categories showed the occupiers organizing movement according to ancestry across a frontier the affected population had not chosen. [17] This provision offered no comparable general mechanism by which Polish or Jewish families could decide the political future of their communities. Nor did its assurances about property protect everyone whose home fell within the new occupation zones. The distinction between an agreement for selected emigrants and the rights of the wider population is important. An official transfer supervised by two governments could receive administrative support, while a refugee trying to return to a relative might face a different and dangerous set of rules. The protocol’s narrow promises cannot be read as a general guarantee of freedom of movement. [17]

The resources and railways inside the bargain

The economic correspondence accompanying the treaty is easily overshadowed by its map. It deserves attention because the new relationship had to function during a continuing European war. In an exchange of letters dated 28 September, the Soviet government committed itself to developing a program of raw-material deliveries, to be compensated by German manufactured goods over a longer period. The parties proposed restoring trade to the highest volume previously reached and beginning negotiations promptly. This was a framework for expanded exchange, rather than a complete list of deliveries already made. [18] Its strategic logic was straightforward. Germany sought resources while facing British and French economic pressure; the Soviet Union sought the industrial products Germany could supply. Their unequal delivery schedules also mattered. Raw materials could support current production, while complex manufactured goods took time to build and deliver. Agreeing to that sequence created both an opportunity for Germany and a question of performance for Moscow. Cooperation therefore involved continuing bargaining over what each side would receive and when, rather than an uncomplicated flow of Soviet assistance. [18] [19] The confidential companion letter made the geography more concrete. Moscow undertook to facilitate German transit toward Romania by the Upper Silesia–Lemberg–Kolomea railway route, and also transit to and from Iran, Afghanistan and the Far East. It offered additional petroleum corresponding to the annual output of the Drohobycz–Borysław oil district, with half supplied from that district and half from other Soviet fields. Germany would compensate with coal and steel piping. The arrangement did not simply give Germany all the oil produced in the occupied district. It used that output as a measure for a promised quantity, while specifying two sources of supply. [20]

Poland refuses to disappear

The clearest Polish answer arrived in the language of diplomacy rather than a battlefield communiqué. On 30 September, Ambassador Jerzy Potocki informed the United States, on his government’s instructions, that the Moscow agreement violated existing treaties and international law. Poland refused to recognize it and intended to recover its occupied territory and its people’s freedom and self-determination. The note was short, direct and addressed to another government. Its significance lay partly in the ordinary diplomatic act itself: the representative of the allegedly extinguished state was continuing to speak and be received as its representative. [2] Institutional continuity had to be maintained under exceptionally difficult conditions. Poland’s senior authorities had entered Romania and been interned. Diplomatic communications between the interned leadership and Polish politicians in France helped make a constitutional succession possible. The Polish foreign ministry’s historical account emphasizes the role of Ambassador Roger Raczyński in sustaining those contacts and securing President Ignacy Mościcki’s transfer of office to Władysław Raczkiewicz. Government survived through decisions, correspondence and recognition, not through the automatic preservation of functioning offices inside the occupied country. [21] On 30 September, Raczkiewicz became president in exile and General Władysław Sikorski became prime minister in France. The government’s initial base was France; its move to Britain followed France’s defeat in 1940. Keeping that sequence clear matters because the familiar phrase “London government” can obscure the immediate effort to reconstitute Polish authority in the autumn of 1939. The leaders now operating abroad were trying to preserve a state that had lost the ability to protect people at home. Their continued existence offered no immediate relief at a checkpoint, but it ensured that military defeat did not become an uncontested diplomatic surrender. [22] The United States gave an explicit answer of its own. A statement issued by Secretary of State Cordell Hull on 2 October affirmed that Washington continued to regard the Polish government as existing despite Poland’s subjection to force. The statement is recorded in an editorial note in the State Department’s documentary collection. Recognition was not military rescue, and the United States remained outside the European war. Nevertheless, this position contradicted the legal and political premise on which Berlin and Moscow had presented their settlement. The continued war against Germany and the survival of Polish diplomacy meant that the partition remained internationally disputed. [23]

London and Paris read the same treaty differently

The joint declaration issued with the treaty tried to turn the occupation of Poland into an argument for ending the European war. Germany and the Soviet Union announced that their settlement had created the basis for peace in eastern Europe, called for an end to the conflict between Germany and the Western powers, and assigned Britain and France responsibility if efforts to end it failed. They also promised consultation about further measures. The sequence of the argument was convenient for both signatories: their conquests were treated as settled before the opponents of those conquests were invited to make peace. [24] On 3 October, Neville Chamberlain described the agreement in the House of Commons as an attempted fourth partition of Poland. He identified the frontier settlement, the peace declaration and the projected economic relationship as connected developments. Britain, he argued, had entered the war against a recurring pattern of German aggression; Poland’s defeat had not removed that reason. His response rejected the suggestion that successful conquest entitled Germany to dictate when the international consequences of its attack should end. The speech also made clear that further promises from Hitler’s government would be judged against its record of broken undertakings. [25] The parliamentary discussion was less uniform than that central statement suggests. In the same debate, David Lloyd George urged a different treatment of the Soviet role, while Labour’s David Grenfell condemned the Soviet intervention and argued that the presence of two aggressors did not diminish the wrong done to Poland. The exchange illustrates a continuing difficulty for British politics: opposition to Germany did not produce a single view of Moscow. Arguments about Soviet security, former imperial frontiers and future strategic rivalry could coexist with recognition that the Soviet Union had participated in Poland’s destruction. [25] Private British assessments were cautious about predicting an unlimited alliance. Joseph Kennedy’s report of 30 September described Foreign Office officials as expecting Moscow to benefit from a prolonged conflict among the Western powers while remaining outside that war. They considered direct Soviet military commitment to Germany unlikely, though the warmth of Ribbentrop’s reception caused concern. The British ambassador in Moscow even raised the possible value of trade incentives in influencing Soviet conduct. These were judgments about interests and possible policy, not privileged knowledge of Stalin’s future decisions. They help explain how condemnation of the partition could coexist with efforts to avoid extending the war to the Soviet Union. [26] French assessments reveal how uncertainty could exaggerate the perceived threat. On 30 September, senior foreign-ministry official Alexis Léger told American ambassador William Bullitt that the Soviet Union had promised Germany 2,000 bombers for an attack on France. Bullitt questioned the claim. The cable documents French anxiety, not the existence of the bomber commitment: an alarming report in a diplomatic archive remains a report requiring corroboration. [27] French concern did not immediately produce a decision to break with Moscow. On 7 October, the French chargé there told Steinhardt that the developing partnership had caused him to reconsider his earlier opposition to a rupture. He was contemplating recommending a firmer policy, potentially including a break in relations, and asked how American representation of French interests might be arranged. He expressly described the inquiry as anticipatory. Preserving that qualification matters: a diplomat exploring a contingency was not announcing a decision by his government. [28] Publicly, Édouard Daladier insisted on security that would last. Chamberlain’s statement of 12 October, replying to Hitler’s subsequent peace proposals, cited the French premier’s broadcast two days earlier and stressed the need for dependable guarantees. Britain and France would not accept conquest as a sufficient foundation for peace merely because Germany now offered negotiations. Their position sustained the war against Germany, although it had not saved Poland from occupation. For Poles, that distinction was painfully concrete: continued allied belligerency preserved a future possibility of liberation while leaving the immediate balance of force inside their country unchanged. [29]

Selling the peace in Germany and the Soviet Union

The German government had a domestic audience for its peace initiative as well as a foreign one. Reports assembled by SOPADE, the German Social Democrats in exile, described hopes that the defeat of Poland would allow the war to end quickly. The reports also recorded reluctance toward a wider conflict and popular irritation with wartime restrictions. They came from opponents of the Nazi regime using incomplete underground reporting, so they cannot be treated as a representative opinion poll. They do, however, challenge the image of a German public uniformly eager for a prolonged European war. [30] Moscow’s public language moved decisively in support of the relationship. In his speech to the Supreme Soviet on 31 October, Molotov defended German–Soviet friendship and presented Germany as seeking peace while Britain and France pursued the war for imperial aims. Steinhardt’s report noted Molotov’s argument that a strong Germany was necessary for European peace, together with his favorable account of the ongoing economic negotiations. This was an official justification of policy, not evidence that ordinary Soviet citizens had reached the same conclusions. It showed the Soviet leadership lending its authority to the diplomatic argument Germany wanted the Western powers to accept. [31]

The boundary as people encountered it

For refugees, the settlement could turn a temporary flight into an indefinite separation. People who had moved east to escape the German advance now faced an emerging barrier across the country. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum records guarded crossings, arbitrary violence and the danger of travelling without papers. Some exhausted refugees returned towards German-held territory because home and family seemed preferable to remaining without money or a destination. These were decisions made under immediate pressure and incomplete knowledge, not informed choices between the later histories of two occupation systems. [32] The confidential population protocol did not provide a general right for everyone to return home. Its selected categories—ethnic Germans departing the Soviet sphere, and Ukrainians and Belarusians departing the German sphere—served the occupiers’ demographic interests. People outside those categories still needed to find a permissible route, obtain documents or attempt an unauthorized crossing. A railway connection discussed as an economic benefit in Moscow could be a blocked route to relatives for someone living beside it. The same settlement that sought predictable movement for specified goods and populations could make ordinary civilian movement much less predictable. [17] [20] Przemyśl makes these changes tangible. German forces had occupied the city before the revised partition placed its principal part under Soviet control. Yad Vashem’s account records German killings of Jews and the burning of synagogues, followed under Soviet authority by the dissolution of Jewish political parties and the subordination of communal institutions to municipal control. Some synagogues continued religious and relief work. Relief at the departure of perpetrators of immediate violence could therefore coexist with fear of the new authorities and the loss of independent organization. Neither response can be converted into a general verdict on how all Jews, Poles or Ukrainians experienced the change. [33] The treaty distributed control without creating the complete administrative machinery through which either occupier would govern. Germany’s annexation measures and the General Government belonged to the following month; the Soviet incorporation measures followed on **1–2 November**. Keeping those steps separate explains what the September agreement achieved: it reduced conflict between the invaders over their respective territorial claims, leaving each substantial room to impose its own institutions. The [study of 26 October](/articles/german-occupation-administration-1939-10-26) examines the resulting German arrangements and the parallel Soviet process. [1] [34]

A settlement Poland refused

The language of friendship expressed practical cooperation: a territorial bargain, suppression of Polish political activity, arrangements for population movement and promises of economic exchange. None required the partners to share an ideology or trust one another indefinitely. The public declaration also tried to make Britain and France responsible for continuing a war that German aggression had begun. Its political purpose was to convert possession into an accepted result while the costs of conquest were still being imposed on Poland’s inhabitants. [24] [17] Poland’s rejection exposed the central weakness in that claim of finality. Berlin and Moscow could arrange withdrawals, assign territory and regulate movement; they could not supply the consent of the state whose land they divided. The government reconstructed in France and its continuing diplomatic recognition preserved that opposition beyond the defeat of the field armies. For the people now living on either side of the boundary, however, the dispute over legitimacy offered little immediate protection. Their next encounter with partition would often be an official demanding papers, property or work—the everyday exercise of the power that the treaty had helped organize. [2] [23]
author: R.G. Cruise
location: Moscow, occupied Poland and the European capitals
summary: The revised frontier was only part of the bargain. Secret protocols, resource agreements and a peace initiative reveal how Germany and the Soviet Union sought to consolidate their conquests—and how Poland refused to accept its disappearance.

sourceMethod: The study checks the supplied dossier against published treaty texts, German diplomatic records, contemporary American cables, parliamentary proceedings, museum research and peer-reviewed scholarship. Official justifications, diplomatic predictions and retrospective testimony are identified as such. The French premier’s October broadcast is cited through the British parliamentary record. Transcriptions were consulted rather than original manuscript images. Selected migration provisions are distinguished from subsequent deportations; signature, ratification, demarcation and annexation are dated separately.
